title: Question 5
stem:
The variation with time $t$ of the voltage level of part of an analogue signal is shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

The signal is sampled at $0.25\text{ ms}$ intervals. Each sample is converted into a four-bit digital number.

Fig. 5.2 lists various times $t$ at which the voltage level is sampled. The digital number for time $t = 0$ is shown.

{{figure:figure_5_2}}

Fig. 5.2

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 5.2, underline the most significant bit (MSB) for the digital number at time $t = 0$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about ordinary decimal numbers - which digit changes the value most if you change it, the left-most or the right-most? Apply the same idea to the 4-bit binary number.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What MSB Means**
Think of binary just like decimal place value. In $1011$ the four positions from left to right have values $8, 4, 2, 1$. The left-most bit is worth $8$, so changing it changes the total most. That is the Most Significant Bit.

Step 2: **Apply to t = 0**
The number is $1011$. The left-most digit is $1$. So you underline that first $1$: $\underline{1}011$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Complete Fig. 5.2 for the times shown.
hints: Hint 1: For each time in Fig. 5.2, read the voltage level straight up from the time axis to the curve in Fig. 5.1, then across to the voltage level axis.
Hint 2: Check how voltage level links to binary using the t = 0 example: level 11 gives 1011. Convert each new level you read to 4-bit binary.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the Sampled Levels**
You are sampling the smooth curve at fixed times. Read $y$-value at each $t$ from Fig. 5.1. You get about: $t=0$ gives $11$, $t=0.25$ gives $6$, $t=0.50$ gives $8$, $t=0.75$ gives $14$, $t=1.00$ gives $5$, $t=1.25$ gives $3$, $t=1.50$ gives $1$.

Step 2: **Convert Level to 4-bit Binary**
The voltage level is just the decimal value of the 4-bit number. For example $11 = 8+2+1 = 1011$. Do the same for the rest: $$6 = 4+2 = 0110$$ $$8 = 8 = 1000$$ $$14 = 8+4+2 = 1110$$ $$5 = 4+1 = 0101$$ $$3 = 2+1 = 0011$$ $$1 = 1 = 0001$$

Step 3: **Fill the Table**
Put those numbers in order under 0.25 ms to 1.50 ms. That completes Fig. 5.2.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
After transmission of the digital numbers, the signal is passed through a digital-to-analogue converter (DAC).

On Fig. 5.3, plot the transmitted analogue signal from the DAC.

{{figure:figure_5_3}}

Fig. 5.3

markscheme_points.text: sketch: 6 horizontal steps of width 0.25 ms shown
steps at correct heights and all steps shown
steps shown in correct time intervals

hints: Hint 1: Remember what a DAC does - it holds each sampled value constant until the next sample arrives, so think about what shape that produces rather than a smooth curve.
Hint 2: Use your binary numbers from (a)(ii) as the heights, with each value lasting for one sampling interval starting at its sample time.
Hint 3: Check the axes of Fig. 5.3 - each horizontal section should be 0.25 ms wide and centred on the integer voltage levels 11, 6, 8, 14, 5, 3, 1.
parts.proper_answer: Staircase of 7 horizontal levels held for 0.25 ms each: 11 from 0 to 0.25 ms, 6 from 0.25 to 0.50 ms, 8 from 0.50 to 0.75 ms, 14 from 0.75 to 1.00 ms, 5 from 1.00 to 1.25 ms, 3 from 1.25 to 1.50 ms, 1 from 1.50 ms onwards.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why It Is a Staircase**
The DAC can only output the last digital value it received. It cannot guess what happened between samples. So from $t = 0$ to $t = 0.25$ ms it holds level $11$ constant, then jumps to the next value. That gives flat steps, not a smooth curve.

Step 2: **Plot Each Step at the Right Height**
Convert your binaries back to levels: $1011=11$, $0110=6$, $1000=8$, $1110=14$, $0101=5$, $0011=3$, $0001=1$. Draw a horizontal line at each of those voltage levels.

Step 3: **Put Each Step in the Right Time Slot**
Each step is $0.25$ ms wide: $$11 \text{ for } 0 \le t < 0.25$$ $$6 \text{ for } 0.25 \le t < 0.50$$ $$8 \text{ for } 0.50 \le t < 0.75$$ $$14 \text{ for } 0.75 \le t < 1.00$$ $$5 \text{ for } 1.00 \le t < 1.25$$ $$3 \text{ for } 1.25 \le t < 1.50$$ $$1 \text{ for } t \ge 1.50$$ Vertical jumps join the steps at the sample times.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The transmitted signal in (b) has less detail than the original signal in Fig. 5.1.

Suggest and explain two means by which the level of detail in the transmitted signal could be increased.

markscheme_points.text: so that step width/depth is reduced
increase number of bits (in each number)
so that step height is reduced

hints: Hint 1: Look at your staircase in (b) - in what two ways does it differ from the smooth original: think about horizontal direction (time) and vertical direction (voltage).
Hint 2: To make the steps narrower in time so fast changes are not missed, what would you change about how often you sample?
Hint 3: To make the steps shorter in height so the voltage is more exact, what would you change about the digital numbers themselves?
Hint 4: For each change, link it clearly to step width or step height to explain why detail improves.
parts.proper_answer: 1. Increase sampling frequency (sample at intervals < 0.25 ms) so step width is reduced and the signal is followed more closely in time. 2. Increase number of bits per sample (> 4 bits) so voltage step height / quantisation interval is reduced and the signal is followed more closely in voltage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Two Types of Lost Detail**
The staircase loses detail in two ways. Horizontally, rapid ups and downs between samples are missed. Vertically, the true voltage is rounded to the nearest whole level, e.g. 14.6 becomes 14. This rounding is quantisation error.

Step 2: **Improve Time Detail - Sample Faster**
Sample more often, i.e. increase sampling frequency or sampling rate, for example every $0.10$ ms instead of $0.25$ ms. Each held value lasts for a shorter time, so the width of each step is reduced and the reconstructed curve follows rapid changes in Fig. 5.1 much better.

Step 3: **Improve Voltage Detail - Use More Bits**
Use more bits per sample, e.g. 8 bits instead of 4 bits. With 4 bits you have only $2^4 = 16$ levels (0 to 15). With more bits you have many more levels with smaller gaps between them. So the height of each voltage step is reduced, rounding error is smaller, and the reconstructed levels sit closer to the true analogue voltages.
